introduction.p: A definite integral gives a number. An indefinite integral denotes the family of antiderivatives of a function. On an interval, all antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant. We will use this fact to write and check indefinite-integral formulas.

paragraphs.title: Definite versus indefinite
paragraphs.p: A definite integral has limits:
It is a number.
An indefinite integral has no limits:
It is a family of functions.

p.em: Definite integral: number. Indefinite integral: family of antiderivatives.

exercise.title: Why is an antiderivative never alone?

statement.p: The functions x^3/3, x^3/3+7, and x^3/3-100 all have the same derivative. In your own words, why does a derivative forget vertical shifts, and why does the indefinite integral therefore name a whole family rather than one function?

hint.p: Differentiating a constant gives zero. So adding a constant cannot change the slope function, and every slope function comes with a stack of parallel graphs.

exercise.title: Why does same derivative means differ by a constant need an interval?

statement.p: A function can have derivative zero on (-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty) without being a single constant on its whole domain. In your own words, why does the constant of integration have to be understood on one connected interval?

hint.p: The Mean Value Theorem compares two points that can be joined inside the domain. Separate pieces of the domain can carry separate constants.

subsection.title: Initial value problems
subsection.p: An indefinite integral gives a family. A starting value chooses one member of the family.

exercise.title: What does an initial value do to a family of antiderivatives?

statement.p: Velocity determines the shape of a position graph, but not where that graph sits vertically. In your own words, why does a starting value F(a)=F_0 select one member of the family F(x)+C?

hint.p: The indefinite integral leaves one free constant. A point on the graph pins that constant down.

subsection.title: Basic antiderivative formulas
subsection.p: Every antiderivative formula can be checked by differentiating the right-hand side.
The first formulas reverse the derivative rules we already know.

p.me: \begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{integrand} \amp \textbf{indefinite integral}\\ \hline 0 \amp \displaystyle C\\ k \amp \displaystyle kx+C\\ x^n,\ n\neq -1 \amp \displaystyle \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\\ \dfrac1x \amp \displaystyle \ln|x|+C\\ e^x \amp \displaystyle e^x+C\\ a^x,\ a>0,\ a\neq1 \amp \displaystyle \frac{a^x}{\ln a}+C \end{array}

exercise.title: What is the difference between a definite integral and an indefinite integral?

statement.p: One object is \int_a^b f(x)\,dx and the other is \int f(x)\,dx. In your own words, why is the first a number and the second a family of functions, even though the same integral sign appears in both?

hint.p: Limits of integration turn accumulation into a completed amount. Removing the limits asks for all functions whose derivative is the integrand.

exercise.title: Why is having an antiderivative different from finding a formula?

statement.p: The integral \int 2x\cos(x^2)\,dx is a reverse chain rule, but \int \cos(x^2)\,dx has no elementary antiderivative. In your own words, why can Part I still guarantee that \int_0^x \cos(t^2)\,dt is a real function with a known derivative?

hint.p: Existence means some function has the desired slope. A usable elementary formula is an extra gift that the basic library does not always provide.
